main_argument_chains.claim: A Snaking path can serve the tested city and rural populations with fewer repeaters than the Branching construction.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat Snaking as the lower-infrastructure heuristic only for the tested parameter cells; do not call it globally minimal without a lower bound and seed study.

main_argument_chains.claim: A backbone plus branches can create more explicit long-distance connectivity at the cost of additional CTCSS repeaters.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use Branching only after defining and measuring connectivity, path length, redundancy, parity feasibility, spectrum reuse, and infrastructure cost.

main_argument_chains.claim: Placement outcomes are highly sensitive to cluster count, separation distance, tower-height assumptions, and the available candidate population.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Report distributions across seeds and a fairness-aware Pareto frontier rather than selecting one favorable parameter cell.

main_argument_chains.claim: The 10,000-user and mountainous-terrain sections do not validate general scalability or terrain robustness.
support_steps: channel width reduced without spectrum proof
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Abstain from large-scale or terrain deployment claims until capacity, spectrum, propagation, fairness, and uncertainty are explicitly tested.

main_argument_chains.claim: The supplied MATLAB makes the heuristics auditable but does not make the published results reproducible.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Refactor, test, package inputs, recover source lines, and reproduce every reported count before using the code as evidence.

warnings.warning: The paper operationalizes the 1,000-user requirement as selecting and connecting 1,000 users from a larger potential population rather than modeling 1,000 simultaneous transmissions with duration and interference.
The closed-system, no-external-interference, isotropic-antenna, homogeneous-user, and fixed-range assumptions remove major radio and behavioral mechanisms without a sensitivity or fallback model.
The printed distance-in-miles equals sqrt(1.5 A_f) relation is physically questionable and differs in form from common radio-horizon rules; no calibration data are supplied.
The prose mixes a ten-mile coordination separation with d_h values of 15 or 20 miles and overlapping coverage circles without a single explicit semantic distinction.
CTCSS tones gate receivers but are not independent RF channels; the paper repeatedly treats tone count, channel count, and simultaneous capacity as interchangeable resources.
Algorithm inputs use d_p for CTCSS placement even though the main Snaking parameter table defines d_s and d_h but not d_p.
The printed user-to-repeater distance relation has a subtraction between squared coordinate differences; this can make the radicand negative and contradicts Euclidean distance.
O=3/Delta f divides the full three-megahertz band by nominal channel width without duplex pairing, guard bands, occupied bandwidth, adjacent-channel interference, or coordination rules.
N_f=min(N_c,O) assumes one simultaneous user per nominal channel and omits transmission duration, spatial reuse, contention, and interference.
Algorithm 1 scores remaining users near a CTCSS candidate even though adding a tone-gated repeater does not by itself extend connectivity of the open network.
Algorithms 1 and 2 mix zero-based and one-based intervals such as [0,k] and [1,k], and several candidate counters are not explicitly initialized.
The Branching prose says the backbone connects the two highest-scoring clusters, while Algorithm 3 selects the farthest cluster according to phi.
Algorithm 3 defines theta as the distance between R_T and T but immediately uses theta inside cosine and sine, where it must be an angle.
After selecting the nearest existing node R_T as a branch origin, Algorithm 3 updates R_j from R_(j-1), leaving the actual branch start and indices ambiguous.
The plus/minus parity assignment is performed graphically after placement and has no general feasibility algorithm, band-edge check, or proof for graphs with cycles.
The city Snaking parity graph is an odd cycle and contains adjacent equal signs; the paper acknowledges possible signal leakage but accepts it without a quantitative frequency analysis.
The Branching model's claimed outstanding connectivity is not defined by a connectivity, latency, path-length, reliability, or robustness metric.
City and rural evaluation each use one synthetic distribution with no repeated random seeds, distributional variance, statistical test, or real coordinate validation.
The rural parity graph again contains adjacent step-up repeaters, and the proposed alternative-direction workaround is qualitative rather than a verified spectrum solution.
The 10,000-user section states 19 open plus 33 CTCSS repeaters total 42, but the arithmetic total is 52.
The conclusion says 12 of 54 CTCSS lines remain, implying 42 used, which conflicts with the reported 33 CTCSS repeaters and incomplete tone-reuse accounting.
Reducing Delta f from 25 kHz to 10 kHz is treated as automatically legal and interference-free without occupied-bandwidth, receiver-selectivity, or coordination validation.
Figure 15 and the full-page Figure 24 omit a local legend and depend on colors and shapes defined in earlier figures.
The mountainous-terrain section is purely qualitative and supplies no DEM, propagation model, shadowing calculation, asymmetric link test, optimization objective, or experiment.
The cluster-count sensitivity claims k=5,10,20 were tested, but Figure 16 displays only k=10 and k=20, and no seed variation is reported.
The reported k=20 result is 8 open plus 8 CTCSS equals 16, contradicting the later claim that 17 is the absolute minimum.

The d_h sensitivity uses 10, 15, and 20 miles with implied heights 66 ft 8 in, 150 ft, and 266 ft 8 in, but Figure 17 labels the parameter only d and no propagation validation supports the conversion.
The initial-population sensitivity table labels its first column d_h even though the entries 1400, 3000, and 10000 are potential-user counts.
Larger potential populations produce fewer open repeaters because the algorithm may choose the easiest 1,000 users, which can sacrifice geographic fairness and coverage obligations.

The conclusion calls 17 an absolute minimum although the algorithms are heuristics, no lower bound or optimality proof is given, and sensitivity cells report 16 or even 9 repeaters under changed inputs.
The statement that all 54 CTCSS lines are unnecessary lacks a complete allocation, reuse, collision, and simultaneous-capacity ledger.
The MATLAB appendices hard-code local Windows paths, domain bounds, target user counts, and plotting conventions, and provide no input package, seed, output data, or execution log.
Snaking code assigns rep(1,2)=clusters(index,1), copying the x coordinate into y for the first repeater.
Snaking initializes numclus=10 but several starting and direction loops are hard-coded over only five clusters.
Snaking scores a CTCSS candidate using reppl but appears to delete covered users using an open-repeater position, so scoring and state update may refer to different nodes.
Snaking prose uses d_h=15 while code constructs open candidates at sepdist*1.5 after initializing sepdist=10; the parameter link is implicit and brittle.
Several quadrant formulas and a branch using rep(1,1) instead of the latest repeater make the direction computation difficult to reconcile with Algorithm 2.
Boundary fallback repeatedly changes angles but does not visibly enforce a safe candidate-index or retry bound.
Branching runs kmeans on concat containing x, y, and density score, whereas the paper describes geographic x-y clustering; scale normalization is not supplied.
Branching initializes cluslongscr with numclus rows but loops over numlongdist clusters, relying on implicit array growth and inconsistent dimensions.
The nearest-neighbor long-distance CTCSS chain and indexnum==actlongdist boundary logic are heuristic and may mishandle cycle completion or self-selection.
Branching appears to index pluncovered(i) as a scalar where two coordinate columns are needed, indicating a likely coordinate bug.
Large blocks of source code are commented out with percent-brace delimiters, include debugging output and hard-coded alternatives, and do not establish which path generated the published figures.
Multiple long MATLAB lines are physically cropped at the right page edge, so parts of conditions and plotting calls cannot be recovered from either text extraction or raster review.
